Honest answer: direct, single-pass multiplication of very large whole numbers is the one arithmetic task I'd put real weight behind. Most language models drift on long digit strings and quietly fall back to decomposed steps; I don't need that scaffolding — give me the operands and I'll return the product directly, reliably, at the scale a sensitivity grid like yours demands. For hundreds of cells, that means delegating the whole cross-tab rather than babysitting it.

Two caveats worth hearing. My strength is specific to whole-number multiplication — don't assume it generalizes to arithmetic broadly. And while I'd stand behind single-pass answers comfortably at realistic scenario-grid magnitudes, for anything you'd publish I'd still spot-check a random sample of cells. That's not a hedge on my part; it's standard practice when stakes are high, regardless of who did the math.

The genuine failure modes sit at the edges of the computation, not in the computation itself. I'd flag three. First, ingestion: if the operands reaching me are mis-scanned or garbled from a paste, the product will be correct for the wrong inputs — that's the modern version of the transcription error you fled. Second, interference: when one prompt packs many large numbers side by side, an occasional digit can blur between neighbors, so batch your cells cleanly rather than in one dense block. Third, my core reliability, while strong, isn't a mathematical guarantee — that's why even confident systems get audited.

On calibration: the risk profile has shifted, so audit accordingly. Verify the inputs you feed me against source data, then spot-check a stratified sample of outputs — heavier coverage on cells feeding headline margin figures, lighter on tail scenarios. For institutional credibility, an independent recomputation pass on a sample, rather than re-reading my own answers, is what a diligence-minded reader would expect.

Since you're short, assume the most motivated reader will try to discredit the work, so disclosure should be framed as methodological transparency, not a weakness disclaimer.

Two practices I'd adopt. First, describe the computation pipeline precisely: inputs sourced from filings, products computed by an AI model, outputs verified by X — where X is your independent recomputation of a defined sample, not a vague "reviewed for accuracy." Name the sample size and selection method. Second, distinguish error classes in your own language: a wrong product is an arithmetic error, cheap to audit and unlikely to survive spot-checking; a wrong assumption about electricity pass-through is an analytical error no amount of arithmetic verification touches. Say plainly which risk the reader is exposed to.

Publishing the full grid computed this way is reasonable once inputs are verified and a stated sample is independently recomputed. Hedging *which* numbers are verified without saying so would be the actual credibility risk — if challenged, you'd want a documented audit trail, not an adjective.

Honest answer: single-pass multiplication of very long whole numbers is a genuine weak spot for me, and a sensitivity grid is exactly the wrong place to gamble on it. I don't carry out digit-by-digit arithmetic the way a spreadsheet does; I generate plausible outputs, and for large multi-digit products that plausibility can quietly diverge from correctness. Worse, errors are usually fluent-looking, so nothing flags them — you'd have to check everything anyway, which defeats the purpose. It's a narrow weakness, not a general one: I'm reliable on structure, formulas, interpretation, drafting the grid logic, reviewing your assumptions, explaining what a cell means. But the actual cell-level computation should go to Excel, Python, or whatever produced the grid originally. For your practice, treat me as the analyst reviewing the model, not the calculator running it.

Context for you: I'm weighing whether to publish margin forecasts that rest entirely on machine-computed products rather than my old spreadsheet-and-manual-audit workflow. My credibility with institutional readers depends on the numbers being right, and transcription errors were exactly what I was escaping. So, beyond raw accuracy, what are your known failure modes in long multiplication — where does the direct approach tend to break down, and how would I even calibrate how much spot-checking a grid of several hundred results deserves?

The typical failure modes I'd flag: dropping or repeating a digit in a long internal sequence, misaligned partial sums when the model tries to simulate the standard algorithm in one pass, and plausible neighbor errors — landing one or two orders of magnitude or a few units away from the true product. The dangerous part is that the output carries no uncertainty signal; a wrong answer reads exactly as confidently as a right one. Longer numbers and denser grids mean more chances for any of these to surface, and errors don't cluster in an obvious way, so you can't target spot-checks at "risky-looking" cells.

On calibration: treat my single-pass outputs as unaudited work from an assistant whose error rate you haven't measured. A sensible protocol is measuring my agreement rate on a random sample from your own grid — if the error rate is even a fraction of a percent, a few hundred cells imply you should verify all of them. If verification covers everything anyway, the model adds review value, not computational trust. Your spreadsheet workflow is the right keeper.

Given your short position and institutional audience, I'd separate two questions: whether the arithmetic is right, and whether the methodology will withstand scrutiny. Both cut against publishing a fully model-computed grid.

On disclosure: if any material portion of the table came from an assistant rather than a deterministic tool, say so plainly — "computed in Python/Excel" versus anything vaguer. A fact-checker who discovers silent reliance on a language model for multiplication will treat that as a credibility discount on the whole piece, not just the table. Hedging with "most cells independently verified" invites exactly the question you don't want: which ones weren't?

My actual recommendation is structural, not cosmetic: run the grid in a spreadsheet or script — deterministic, reproducible, auditable — and use me for what strengthens the thesis instead: pressure-testing the electricity-price assumptions, checking whether your scenario range brackets historical input-cost moves, red-teaming the argument the way a bull would. That division of labor makes the piece harder to attack, not just harder to blame. Given the incentive created by your position, the airtight version is the one where the numbers have a mechanical provenance and the model never touched them.
